answer:
Size the return line for about **270 m³/h** of two-phase flow. Almost all of that volume is flash steam, not liquid. I computed it with CoolProp (IAPWS-97 water properties).

**Basis:** saturated condensate at 10 barg (11.01 bara) flashes adiabatically to 0 barg (1.013 bara). No subcooling and no pressure drop in the return line.

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| Saturation temperature at 11.01 bara | 184.1 °C |
| Enthalpy of saturated liquid at 11.01 bara | 781.3 kJ/kg |
| Enthalpy of saturated liquid at 1.013 bara | 419.1 kJ/kg |
| Heat of vaporisation at 1.013 bara | 2256.5 kJ/kg |
| Flash fraction, x = (781.3 − 419.1)/2256.5 | 0.161 (16.1 %) |
| Flash steam | 160.5 kg/h × 1.673 m³/kg = **268.6 m³/h** |
| Residual liquid at 100 °C | 839.5 kg/h → **0.88 m³/h** |
| **Total volumetric flow** | **≈ 269.5 m³/h (0.075 m³/s)** |

**Why this matters:** the flash steam takes up about 99.7 % of the volume. The liquid alone, about 0.9 m³/h, would suggest a line roughly 300 times too small. Size the line as a two-phase (flash steam) line. A common practice is to keep the steam velocity at about 15 m/s or below, which avoids water hammer and erosion. That points to roughly DN 80. This velocity limit and the line size are typical design practice, not something I calculated in detail.

**Not checked:**
- If the line runs above atmospheric pressure (back-pressure or line losses), less condensate flashes and the steam is denser, so the volumetric flow will be lower.
- If the condensate leaves the traps subcooled, the flash fraction is also lower.

So 270 m³/h is the conservative, upper-bound basis.
